extracted.intended_audience: Emerson College community, aspiring comedians, and general readers interested in comedy/career advice
extracted.subtask_short: stand-up comedy craft and career advice
extracted.subtask_description: An interview-style piece offering practical stagecraft and career guidance for stand-up comedians, covering rehearsal frequency, stage presence, deploying personal material, handling bombing, and leveraging new media. Geared toward performers building their craft and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent stage time / deliberate practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicate as much time as possible to developing the craft; perform regularly (e.g., 'I was on stage five to seven nights a week').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro describes intense early practice—riding her bicycle across town to do three- to five-minute sets—emphasizing persistence and repeated live experience to hone material and stage skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace silence and uncomfortable moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use silence and awkwardness deliberately as part of your comedic sensibility ('I think one of my signature qualities on stage is embracing silence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro credits her mother for loving uncomfortable moments and suggests allowing awkwardness to unfold can create funny and revealing beats; silence can be a tactical device rather than something to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be present and work with what's happening
rubrics_metrics.description: Stay present on stage and incorporate current circumstances into your performance ('being present and… using what's happening and what’s around you').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when she forgot parts of her set on Conan, acknowledging the mistake aloud ('OK, I’m forgetting, I’ve forgotten') helped her recover and kept the audience engaged—acknowledgement can bring you back on track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge mistakes openly to mitigate bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set is going poorly, admit what’s happening instead of pretending everything’s fine to reduce escalation of failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro's Conan example shows that transparent acknowledgment ('I’m messing up') can reduce awkwardness and help regain control; treating bombing as a present moment to engage with is preferred to hiding errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take risks by bringing personal truth to material
rubrics_metrics.description: Using deeply personal or risky subject matter on stage (e.g., illness, grief) can be worth the risk if it’s honest ('I went on stage and I talked about it... it felt worth the risk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Her 30-minute Largo set hours after a cancer diagnosis demonstrates that exposing raw personal truth can profoundly connect with audiences, even with the potential to 'bomb terribly and awkwardly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedy as an outlet for processing trauma and life events
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up can be a means to work through grief, illness, breakups, and other personal crises ('doing comedy gave her an outlet to deal with these problems').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro describes multiple simultaneous tragedies and how performing allowed her to talk about them and cope; this frames intimate material as both therapeutic and artistically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and experience build confidence and stage persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence and comfort on stage develop over years of repetition and exposure ('It’s really the repetition and acknowledging that I’m supposed to be here').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro reflects on 25 years of performing and seeing 'glimpses' of earlier selves, arguing sustained practice produces a stronger stage presence and self-assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study influences and mentors to shape sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from comedians you admire to inform your sensibility and approach ('Paula Poundstone, Joan Rivers, Richard Pryor, and Whoopi Goldberg' inspired her).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro recommends dedicating time to craft and cites influential performers; exposure to a range of styles can help a newcomer discover elements to adopt or adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grind/logistical commitment in early career
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to make physical/logistical sacrifices (travel, odd hours) to get stage time early in your career ('I only had a bicycle... ride from Hollywood to Santa Monica').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anecdote underlines the importance of practical determination—showing up, even under difficult conditions, to get micro-sets and build experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage new platforms (podcasts, social media) for growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Use podcasts and social media as additional creative outlets and income sources ('there’s money to be made in this').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro notes surprise at the podcast boom and how audio-only formats can expand reach and financial opportunity; having multiple platforms (her two podcasts) complements live performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective in career choices—recognize what you don't want
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s valuable to discover not only what you want to pursue but also what you don't want to do in your career ('it’s as exciting to realize what you don’t want to do as it is to find out what you do want to do').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaro gives the example of deciding she no longer wants to direct, illustrating that clarity about negative preferences helps shape a sustainable career.
